lede: A sociable, horse-racing, football-loving Kedah prince who took more than twenty years to pass his law exams, then talked the British Empire out of Malaya without a war, and lived to see the country he founded argue fondly and fiercely with him for the rest of his life.

ps: Tunku Abdul Rahman Putra Al-Haj was born on 8 February 1903 in Alor Setar, Kedah, a son of the Sultan of Kedah. 'Tunku' is a royal title, and Malaysians still simply call him the Tunku.

In 1951 he became president of UMNO, the main Malay party, and built the Alliance with Chinese and Indian parties. On 31 August 1957, at Merdeka Stadium in Kuala Lumpur, he declared the independence of the Federation of Malaya, and became its first prime minister.

In 1963 he brought Malaya, Singapore, Sabah and Sarawak together as Malaysia. Singapore left in 1965, and after the violence of May 1969 he stepped down in 1970. He died on 6 December 1990, aged 87, honoured as Bapa Kemerdekaan, the Father of Independence.

His father was Sultan Abdul Hamid Halim Shah of Kedah. His mother, Che Menjalara, came from a Thai noble family. Kedah then owed loyalty to Siam, and only in 1909, when he was six, did a treaty pass it to British protection.
He was one of the Sultan's many children and grew up in the palace with plenty of freedom. As a boy he was sent to school in Bangkok, then to the Penang Free School.

ps.t: In 1920 a Kedah state scholarship took him to St Catharine's College, Cambridge. He later said he was first refused a place in the college's residence because he was not white, and that he protested.
ps.why: His own later recollection; the details are not confirmed by college records we know of.

ps: He took his degree in 1925, then went to London to study law at the Inner Temple. He enjoyed fast cars, horse races and friends more than textbooks, and kept failing his exams. He went home in the early 1930s and served the Kedah government as a district officer, where he came to know the problems of farmers and fishermen first hand.

ps.t: War, December 1941. As Japanese troops invaded Malaya, the British planned to move his elderly father to Penang. The Tunku intercepted the car and took the Sultan back to safety in Kedah, so that the ruler would stay with his people.
ps.why: Told by the Tunku and his biographers; the outline is accepted, the details vary.

ps: The Malayan Union, 1946. After the war Britain tried to merge the Malay states into one colony and reduce the sultans' powers. Malays protested across the country, UMNO was founded under Dato' Onn Jaafar, and the British replaced the plan with the Federation of Malaya in 1948.
Lawyer at last, 1949. He went back to London and was called to the bar at the age of 46. He returned to work as a deputy public prosecutor in Kuala Lumpur.
UMNO, August 1951. When Onn Jaafar left UMNO after it refused to open its membership to non-Malays, the party chose the Tunku as its president.

The Alliance, 1952 to 1954. UMNO and the Malayan Chinese Association, led by Tan Cheng Lock, ran together in the Kuala Lumpur town elections of 1952 and won most seats. The Malayan Indian Congress joined in 1954. The Alliance showed Britain that Malaya's communities could govern together.
The first election, 27 July 1955. The Alliance won 51 of the 52 elected seats in the Federal Legislative Council, and the Tunku became Chief Minister.

Baling, December 1955. He met Chin Peng, leader of the Malayan Communist Party, whose guerrillas had been fighting since 1948, at a school in Baling, Kedah. He offered an amnesty, but not recognition of the party. The talks failed, and the fight went on.

London, early 1956. He led a delegation of Alliance leaders and the rulers' representatives to London, and Britain agreed to independence. Back home, on 20 February 1956, he announced the news to a huge crowd in Melaka.

Merdeka, 31 August 1957. At midnight the British flag came down in Kuala Lumpur. That morning, in the new Merdeka Stadium, he read the Proclamation of Independence and led the crowd in shouts of 'Merdeka!'

Malaysia, 1961 to 1963. In May 1961, in a speech in Singapore, he proposed a larger federation. After talks, a British commission and a UN survey, Malaysia was formed on 16 September 1963. Brunei chose to stay out. Indonesia under Sukarno opposed it with an armed 'Confrontation' that lasted until 1966.

Singapore, 9 August 1965. Tension between Kuala Lumpur and Lee Kuan Yew's People's Action Party grew, and there were deadly riots in Singapore in 1964. The Tunku decided that separation was the only alternative to bloodshed. Singapore became independent, and Lee wept on television.

13 May 1969. After a general election in which the Alliance lost many seats, violence between Malays and Chinese broke out in Kuala Lumpur. The official toll was 196 dead; other estimates are higher. A state of emergency was declared and power passed largely to a National Operations Council under his deputy, Tun Abdul Razak.
Stepping down, 22 September 1970. A few weeks after the national principles of the Rukun Negara were announced, he handed the premiership to Tun Razak.

An independent Malaya won by negotiation, with a written constitution, a king chosen in turn from the nine Malay rulers, and elected government. It was one of the most peaceful handovers from the British Empire.
The Alliance formula: separate parties for each community, sharing power at the top. Its successor, the Barisan Nasional, governed Malaysia until 2018.
Malaysia itself, joining the peninsula with Sabah and Sarawak in Borneo, which is still the shape of the country.

A regional voice: he helped found the Association of Southeast Asia in 1961, a forerunner of ASEAN, and in 1961 joined other Commonwealth leaders in condemning South Africa's apartheid, after which South Africa left the Commonwealth.

After office he became the first Secretary-General of the Organisation of the Islamic Conference (1971 to 1973). Later, in Penang, he wrote newspaper columns for The Star, collected in books such as Looking Back (1977).
Sharifah Rodziah Barakbah, his third wife, married in 1939, a calm partner who supported him through his political life.
Tun Abdul Razak (1922 to 1976), his deputy throughout his years as prime minister and his successor, the organiser to the Tunku's charm.
Tun Dr Ismail Abdul Rahman (1915 to 1973), his trusted minister of home affairs and later deputy prime minister.
Tan Cheng Lock (1883 to 1960), founder of the Malayan Chinese Association, co-architect of the Alliance.
V. T. Sambanthan (1919 to 1979), president of the Malayan Indian Congress, who spoke for the Indian community in the Alliance at independence.
Onn Jaafar (1895 to 1962), founder of UMNO and an early rival.
Lee Kuan Yew (1923 to 2015), Singapore's prime minister, his partner and opponent in the Malaysia years.
Chin Peng (1924 to 2013), communist leader, his opponent at Baling.
He was born when Malaya was a patchwork of British colonies and protected Malay states, rich in tin and rubber, with large Chinese and Indian communities brought in to work them.

The Japanese occupation of 1941 to 1945 broke the idea that Britain could protect Malaya. Afterwards came the Emergency, from 1948 to 1960, a jungle war against communist guerrillas that killed thousands.
Across Asia, India, Burma, Indonesia and others were winning independence, some through long wars. Malaya's leaders chose negotiation, and Britain, tired and stretched, agreed.

His years in power were the Cold War: he stood with the West, but argued for Asian and Muslim solidarity, and loved sport as a way to bring nations together. He led the Asian Football Confederation for many years and started the Merdeka football tournament in 1957.
He is remembered as Bapa Kemerdekaan and Bapa Malaysia. Every 31 August Malaysians watch the old footage of him raising his arm and calling 'Merdeka!'

ps.t: He liked to call himself the happiest prime minister in the world, and many remember his warmth, his jokes and his openness to all communities.
ps.why: A phrase he used himself in speeches and interviews.

ps: In old age he criticised later governments, including Mahathir Mohamad's, and defended the independence of the courts and the press. He was buried in the royal mausoleum at Langgar, near Alor Setar.
His former residence in Kuala Lumpur is now the Memorial Tunku Abdul Rahman Putra, and a university and colleges carry his name.

myths.c: Malaya's independence was won by war.
myths.t: It was negotiated with Britain, through elections and conferences. The communist insurgency was a separate war, which the new government continued to fight until 1960.

myths.c: The Tunku is the face on Malaysian banknotes.
myths.t: The portrait is of Tuanku Abdul Rahman of Negeri Sembilan, the first Yang di-Pertuan Agong, or king. The similar names cause endless confusion.

myths.c: He threw Singapore out in anger.
myths.t: Separation came after two years of bitter disputes and riots. The Tunku saw it as the way to avoid wider bloodshed. Historians still argue how much each side wanted it.

myths.c: 13 May 1969 had a single, simple cause.
myths.t: Tension after the election, economic gaps between communities and political rivalry all played a part. The Tunku was blamed by critics within his own party and soon left office, but what started the violence is still debated.
